pr_body:
Adds 3D physics interpolation to the rendering server, based on @lawnjelly's

- https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/52846
- https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/60147

This PR does not yet include support for multimeshes (https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/91818) or particles.

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/assets/229837/57261451-ecab-43c4-b060-77d5ed697d68

To-do:

- [x] Make it compile.
- [x] Make it work.
- [x] Bind some `RenderingServer` methods and add their documentation.
- [x] Include more follow-up fixes/changes that came after the initial PR.
- [x] Test more extensively.

This PR is sponsored by My Spare Time™.

- *Production edit: This closes https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/89846 and
closes https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/2753.*

Hello, I downloaded the artifact and made a test scene with a car. Here is the scene: 
[physics-interpolation-test.zip](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/files/15462915/physics-interpolation-test.zip)

Testing with physics ticks set to 15 Hz, the car handling seems to behave the same with physics interpolation on and off, but the wheels shows in a strange way:

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/assets/67930504/e7363520-8d5f-42fe-bcb4-60ac87656121

There seems some confusion here:

Wheels, helicopters and fast rotating objects cannot easily be natively handled by physics interpolation. I mentioned it here (and several other places if I remember right), although it may not be in the docs yet:

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/52846#issuecomment-979811468
#72207

The problem is that in the `VisualServer` the only information you have for rotation is a basis, which is effectively capped between e.g. 0 and 360 degrees.  The interpolation can only assume a shortest arc between the two most recent samples, e.g. 0-40, 170-190, 350-20 etc.

The problem is that if an object moves more than 180 degrees in one tick, the interpolation will be wrong:

Wheel moves 0-190, the interpolation will be from 190-360 (because that is the shortest arc), i.e. the interpolation will rotate in the opposite direction. You can't use intelligence to decide that from the previous move it is _likely_ to move from 0-190, because, well it _could_ be moving in reality from 190-360, and in some circumstances the intelligent version would be wrong.

So for fast rotating objects you either have to up the tick rate, or turn off physics interpolation for that object and handle it manually on the client side (rather than server). It is possible the vehicle wheel class could be modified to handle this client side.

This has already come up in users games, and they have taken the approach to switch off (using `physics_interpolation_mode`) and handle it manually.

You will probably need to use `get_global_transform_interpolated()` to get the wheels to line up to the interpolated car body (else the wheel positions will not be interpolated, and will lead the car).

So if an explosive force sends a box rotating quickly you'll see interpolation artifacts? Doesn't it mean that you can never be sure and will have to go back to manually interpolating all unconstrained rigid bodies if you want reliable results? Could angular velocities be taken into account when interpolating maybe?

> So if an explosive force sends a box rotating quickly you'll see interpolation artifacts? Doesn't it mean that you can never be sure and will have to go back to manually interpolating all unconstrained rigid bodies if you want reliable results? Could angular velocities be taken into account when interpolating maybe?

Yes, ideally it would be nice to modify the physics / render server to be able to send across something like a delta so we could deal with this problem correctly. The current situation is due to historical design, which didn't foresee physics interpolation.

_A little background_
It took a lot of lobbying / convincing and politics to get physics interpolation into 3.x, so the emphasis had been on minimally intrusive approach. As time has gone on the community has learned that this is not a fringe feature, but essential for most games (in some form - in multiplayer you may use different approach, and pixel perfect games may use different techniques).

So now (in 4.x at least) it is a lot more feasible to consider more intrusive engine changes to make things work as easily as possible for users (like sending delta to `VisualServer`).

On the other hand we have to trade off the engine code complexity and maintenance, as e.g. sending deltas can makes physics interpolation code creep into more areas, and contributors often have to be aware of how it works in order to make changes / not break things, so there is a definite _cost_.

There's the maintenance of 2 paths - with and without interpolation, and we ideally don't want physics interpolation to add a cost to projects that don't want to use it.

>It took a lot of lobbying / convincing and politics to get physics interpolation... as time has gone on the community has learned that this is not a fringe feature, but essential for most games

UPDATE: This turns out to be a bit of bag of worms, as a lot of `Camera` functions are designed without the possibility of physics interpolation. We will discuss best way to proceed on this making it as easy as possible for users.

The core of the problem is that sometimes these `Camera` functions you might want to use interpolated space, and sometimes uninterpolated. (This is why `get_global_transform()` and `get_global_transform_interpolated()` are separate functions, to allow the user to choose explicitly.)

It also ties in with something myself and @rburing were discussing, whether the `Camera` interpolation might be better done scene side rather than server side (this is the case for 2D already).

Here is another test project that shows another potential issue:

[test-physics-interpolation-init.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/15592586/test-physics-interpolation-init.zip)

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/assets/499286/4b27fd02-67d9-483a-9a2e-274853c639e5

Here the camera is moving right 20 m/s without damping or gravity and every 3 seconds a ball is spawned in front of the camera with the same linear velocity as the camera.

The issue here is that when the physics interpolation is enabled the ball appears in a wrong spot initially and then travels to the correct spot. Ideally there should be no movement relative to the camera as the ball maintains the same relative position throughout its lifetime. Project is using 10 physics ticks per second. The ball is spawned in a physics frame and despawn after 2 seconds.

This issue isn't visible when the objects being spawned have zero velocity. The more velocity they have the more distance they appear to travel into the correct position. The issue can also be triggered by calling `reset_physics_interpolation()`.

I also tried Godot 3.6-beta5 and the issue is there too.

I believe this is caused by initially setting `global_xform_prev` to the same value as `global_xform_curr` which is technically correct when the object is not moving but isn't ideal otherwise.

Although there are probably better ways to fix the issue I should probably mention a workaround that I was using in my personal project:
```
spawned_object_interpolation.previous_global_transform.origin -= camera_physics_interpolation.current_global_transform.origin - camera_physics_interpolation.previous_global_transform.origin
```

> Although there are probably better ways to fix the issue I should probably mention a workaround that I was using in my personal project:

See _"Moving Start"_:
https://docs.godotengine.org/en/3.6/tutorials/physics/interpolation/using_physics_interpolation.html#call-reset-physics-interpolation-when-teleporting-objects

You do need to take care though in some situations, because if you estimate the initial velocity of e.g. a missile and move it forward over the first tick, it can potentially tunnel through physics objects. You can alternatively e.g. hide a missile during the first tick, which prevents tunneling but adds a delay.

You are correct, I don't know why it ended up working in the testbed (maybe I had switched interpolation off).
I've identified a couple of problems:
* My earlier test project was wrong, it can't just do a `reset` when you click the button (else you get the streaking, because the position has not been primed). Although maybe that was your intention with the original MRP, that the timeout worked, and the button didn't?
* In the engine, there is a convenience `teleport_list` which screws with the timing.

The `teleport_list` I forgot the exact reason for. It defers the reset until the next physics tick. This was either to prevent jumps on frames, or more likely to ensure the transform had been flushed to the `VisualServer` before the reset. However the existing part of the PR now flushes the transform to the `VisualServer` immediately before calling reset, so this may no longer be necessary.

Indeed just directly resetting in `VisualServer` (`prev = curr`) rather than using the deferred `teleport_list` seems to fix the problem. I'll see whether we can get rid of the teleport lists now for both 3D and 2D if we are going with this approach.

UPDATE:
There is also another bug with the MRP, to do with out of order processing. When e.g. `reset_ball` occurs, it places the ball on that physics tick based on the position of the camera. The problem is that the ball placement can be on tick 6, while the camera is still on tick 5 (it hasn't been physics processed yet).

This is an extremely subtle problem which I'm pretty sure occurs all the time in Godot games, but when the tick rate is high enough you don't notice it. But it shows up in test projects like this (I'm currently running at 1tps).

Also discovered another Godot bug - `get_physics_process_delta_time()` seems to return 0 within the `_ready()` function. :man_facepalming: 

Another bug: The physics tick counter is updated in the wrong place. Essentially at 1 tps and 60fps, a single tick takes place then it increments the tick counter _immediately_ (0 to 1) _before_ doing the frames. So the within the frames, input etc it reports being within tick 1 but tick 1 hasn't started yet. This mostly causes confusion in MRPs, but I'm wondering if this is something we can fix without breaking compat. This is probably causing a bunch of knock on bugs.

For instance, for input if you happen to click within the physics processing, you will get reported as tick 0, but if you click _after_ it will report being in tick 1 when tick 1 hasn't started yet.

@matmas If you can try the latest version of https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/92784 and let me know how you get on that would be great.

There is also a new MRP project which correct quite a few problems with my previous and adds similar tests for the camera:
[Test Physics Interpolation Init3.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/15731412/Test.Physics.Interpolation.Init3.zip)

It does the adding with timer, you can click reset manually, or if you press return it will reset the `Camera` (similar to how it is done for the ball).

BTW the project now derives the positions directly from `Engine.get_physics_frame()` to eliminate order of processing errors. You will need to take account of order of processing if you want to e.g. drive the ball from the camera, because the ball may be moved _before_ the camera has been positioned, so you need to account for this either with scene tree changes or by setting `process_priority`.

There's quite a bit of refactoring under the hood to get the moving starts working correctly, I had forgotten how much deferred stuff Godot does under the hood and we have to work around this.

I tested the latest revision of this PR and while the initial camera position is set correctly now, using `reset_physics_interpolation()` in the player script no longer prevents the camera from following the interpolated position (e.g. when the player falls off the world in Kinematic Character 3D or presses <kbd>R</kbd> to respawn).

Also, in Truck Town, `reset_physics_interpolation()` works to prevent the camera from interpolating when it's changed by the player when pressing <kbd>C</kbd>, but only if the node's top-level status isn't changed at the same time. This means the reset works when going from Exterior to Interior, but not from Interior to Top-Down or from Top-Down to Exterior.

One thing I noticed in your test project is that the SpawnTimer has process_mode set to _Idle_ while both my Godot 3 and 4 versions have it set to _Physics_. This difference seems to be the cause of the streaks you observed even when interpolation is turned off.

Another thing to keep in mind is the difference between Godot 3 and 4. In order to spawn a RigidBody with desired velocity and position in Godot 3 one needs add `linear_velocity * get_physics_process_delta_time()` to its `position`. This is not needed in Godot 4 so if we choose to do it anyway in order to avoid streaks we also need to compensate for it by subtracting by the same amount before.

I have tested your test project with the following diff and it solves the streaks:

```diff
diff --git a/main.gd b/main.gd
index 9720449..a7abc4b 100644
--- a/main.gd
+++ b/main.gd
@@ -10,6 +10,7 @@ func _on_SpawnTimer_timeout() -> void:
    ball.position = camera_body.position + Vector3.FORWARD * 2
    ball.linear_velocity = camera_body.linear_velocity
    add_child(ball)
+   ball.position -= ball.linear_velocity * get_physics_process_delta_time()
    ball.reset_physics_interpolation()
    ball.position += ball.linear_velocity * get_physics_process_delta_time()
 
diff --git a/main.tscn b/main.tscn
index bab659a..46e9fdd 100644
--- a/main.tscn
+++ b/main.tscn
@@ -38,6 +38,7 @@ shape = SubResource("1")
 [node name="Camera3D" type="Camera3D" parent="CameraBody"]
 
 [node name="SpawnTimer" type="Timer" parent="."]
+process_callback = 0
 wait_time = 3.0
 autostart = true
```

Remember there are a lot of use cases for `get_global_transform_interpolated()`, many of which might assume a standing start. The suggestion that all objects should be assumed to start moving with the camera seems somewhat strange, imo.

Placing objects with a moving start requires some understanding of how interpolation works (with previous and current transforms), I'm not sure there is an easy way around this.

We could potentially have helper API functions to initially place objects with a velocity, e.g.
`set_global_transform_interpolated(Vector3 start_pos, Vector3 start_vel)`, that handle the resets for you, if that would be easier for users to understand. (I think we did discuss this _way back_, but it was figured that `reset_physics_interpolation()` would cover most use cases, at least to start with.)

But for priming client interpolated objects, you would have to prime before this call. An alternative would be to have a bool on `Spatial`s that forced them to start with client side interpolation.

The situation with client interpolation and priming is somewhat of a pain, but it's a consequence of the design - interpolation is usually done server side, and the server may be operating out of sync with the client (scene tree), so we can't query the server positions (because that would cause a stall as it would require flushing the pipeline). Client side interpolation is thus a parallel system that mimicks what is happening on the server, in order to allow scene objects to track other interpolated scene objects.

> Sometimes I get the following warning when running this project:

You are getting the warning because you shouldn't be doing this. If you want to move a camera in process, set the interpolation mode for the node to OFF. If you want to use interpolation, move the camera in `_physics_process()`, and it will interpolate.

If you move an interpolated `Camera` during `_process()`, it will at best overwrite the current transform, and result in strange jittering. It is possible to move `Camera` during `_process()` for initial placement, but you may need to use `reset_physics_interpolation()`.

> As you said the relative locations move a bit and since this time the NinePatchRect is also paused it doesn't always stay centered on the ball depending when you pause the game relative to the physics frame boundary.

The problem here is the physics interpolation fraction, because some objects in the scene tree will be paused and some will contrinue to move. A possible way around this would be to have a main physics interpolation fraction, and a paused physics interpolation fraction, and pick the correct one depending on where it is called.

This is maybe doable, by changing all the calls to `Engine::get_physics_interpolation_fraction()` to e.g. local functions on the node that query the pause state and return either this or a paused fraction, or adding a bool parameter to `get_physics_interpolation_fraction()` to return whether it is unpaused or paused (presumably with a default to unpaused).

This does however push complexity to the many calling sites, and may be more bug prone and require more maintenance, and we'd have to see whether this trade off was worth it, versus having a small visual change in certain projects (as you show), just during the pause / unpause at low tick rates.

It also relies on there being no changes to the pausing system. At the moment we have a single global pause, but if they wanted to add e.g. different types of pause, or change the pause state of objects during the pause, it would break. Whereas resetting is a little clunky (I'll give you that) but it *just works* :tm: .

It's possible we can investigate the other method, but it's not massive high priority (there are likely other more important interpolation bugs to address first).

For scenarios where you don't want physics interpolation (or want to do your own custom interpolation), you can selectively disable interpolation on a node by node basis, and all its children inherit this property (by default):
![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/ce35db2f-646b-48fd-b0f9-4842a5fd3d69)

In fact, even if physics interpolation is enabled in the project, if your root node has the physics interpolation property turned off (and all other nodes are left at default), it'll be functionally similar to having physics interpolation disabled.

Given these facts, I can see a better argument for having (project) physics interpolation enabled by default. The scenarios where a user would benefit from interpolation far outnumber the scenarios where users would want interpolation off. And in the scenarios where you would want interpolation off, it's far better to disable interpolation for the specific nodes involved in said scenario, rather than turning it off for the entire project.

The main problem is the user has to KNOW they're using Physics Interpolation, something a Beginner WILL NOT KNOW, nor be informed of the implications of using it, and you totally missed the point of the 2 examples I've given above.
I know that that function exists, I also know that I can disable Physics Interpolation and do my custom logic easily.

A User that doesn't even KNOW they're using Physics Interpolation will not KNOW that they need to reset physics interpolation when teleporting, nor that there may be cases where they need to write their own Interpolation Logic, simply because they won't even KNOW that they're using the Feature, It'll just Manifest to them as Bugs that'll needlessly frustrate the unaware users

Physics Interpolation can be Heavily Recommended in the Documentation with getting started (and project setting) and all with all the relevant links to the documentation regarding proper usage, but it cannot be stressed enough, this **CANNOT** be on by default.

Don't get me wrong, I'd love to have Physics Interpolation as Standard, but this cannot be enforced by Godot, as Godot can only enforce things that are blatantly obvious to the user, or things that "Just Work"

> The main problem is the user has to KNOW they're using Physics Interpolation, something a Beginner WILL NOT KNOW, nor be informed of the implications of using it, and you totally missed the point of the 2 examples I've given above. I know that that function exists, I also know that I can disable Physics Interpolation and do my custom logic easily.
> 
> A User that doesn't even KNOW they're using Physics Interpolation will not KNOW that they need to reset physics interpolation when teleporting, nor that there may be cases where they need to write their own Interpolation Logic, simply because they won't even KNOW that they're using the Feature, It'll just Manifest to them as Bugs that'll needlessly frustrate the unaware users
> 
> Physics Interpolation can be Heavily Recommended in the Documentation with getting started (and project setting) and all with all the relevant links to the documentation regarding proper usage, but it cannot be stressed enough, this **CANNOT** be on by default.
> 
> Don't get me wrong, I'd love to have Physics Interpolation as Standard, but this cannot be enforced by Godot, as Godot can only enforce things that are blatantly obvious to the user, or things that "Just Work"

I am not entirely convinced that having it enabled by default is the correct thing, but this argument does not make much sense. There are thousands of things a Godot beginner will also not KNOW, and that's why the documentation exists. In contrast, how many "camera jitter bugs" would go away if interpolation was on by default? It seems like a rite of passage that could easily be dealt with now.

A Godot beginner will most likely go through the "Getting Started" articles, so why can't we respect them a bit more and assume they will also read a big warning note if it is added there?

issue_context.title: Physics interpolation is not implemented for 3D
issue_context.body:
### Tested versions

Reproducible in: 4.0-alpha1 - 4.3.dev5
Not reproducible in: 3.5-beta2 - 3.6-beta4

### System information

Godot v4.3.dev (99ff024f7) - Ubuntu 22.04.4 LTS 22.04 - X11 - GLES3 (Compatibility) - NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2060 with Max-Q Design - AMD Ryzen 9 4900HS with Radeon Graphics (16 Threads)

### Issue description

The project setting `physics/common/physics_interpolation` and the node property `physics_interpolation_mode` have no effect on 3D nodes such as physics bodies moved in `_physics_process`.

I could use an addon like https://github.com/lawnjelly/smoothing-addon/tree/4.x, but I would prefer a built-in solution.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Run the attached MRP which has its physics tick rate set to 20 ticks per second and physics interpolation enabled.
2. Notice the 3D scene does not look smooth.

### Minimal reproduction project (MRP)

[physics-interpolation-3d-test.zip](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/files/14734983/physics-interpolation-3d-test.zip)

- *Production edit: Related to https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/2753.*

review_comments: I prefer it the way it is. I implemented all your other style suggestions, thanks!

This function seems to be called twice per process frame - once here and the other time due to calling `tree->client_physics_interpolation_add_node_3d(...)` at the end of this function. Since `update_client_physics_interpolation_data()` is not idempotent the variables `global_xform_curr` and `global_xform_prev` will end up having same value which results this function returning transforms that are not interpolated as `(a + (b - a) * f` equals `a` when `a == b`.
Yes but see the method, it doesn't update the previous if it's on the same tick, right?

It is often called twice, yes. The function contains a tick counter which ensures it only operates _once_ per tick.

The data must get updated, but if `get_global_transform_interpolated()` is called before the tick update, it is refreshed early. The logic admittedly isn't super clear, but it works this way to prevent an order of operations bug.

Yes, it is true that `global_xform_prev` is updated only once per tick.

The not so obvious thing is that when `update_client_physics_interpolation_data()` gets called from `SceneTree::ClientPhysicsInterpolation::physics_process()`, the function `Engine::get_singleton()->get_physics_frames()` is returning incorrect value due to being updated late. This way the newly changed value from `get_global_transform()` is stored into `global_xform_curr` even before we actually change `global_xform_prev`. The next call to `update_client_physics_interpolation_data()` from `get_global_transform_interpolated()` we finally see that the tick has changed and we set `global_xform_prev` to `global_xform_curr` which is the same as `get_global_transform()` and so both `global_xform_prev` and `global_xform_curr` end up having the same value.
